title: Can an Egyptian numeral use one symbol ten or more times?
description: The board looks at what ten copies of one Egyptian symbol are worth, and why a numeral never keeps them. A number such as three hundred twenty four is used to check the idea.
teaching_notes: One idea: ten of any landmark make exactly one of the next, so a numeral always regroups them. Watch for students who think a long row of the same symbol is a proper numeral.

source: Figure it Out (bases and their limits, question 1)
video_script.why: The child uses the idea from the base five example, that five of a shape are always regrouped, for the Egyptian system with ten.
video_script.substitution: Instead of five of a shape making the next one, ten of an Egyptian symbol make the next one.
video_script.anchor: the book's Egyptian number system, where each landmark is ten times the one before
video_script.payoff_line: No, ten of any symbol make one of the next landmark, so they are always regrouped.

final_answer.value: No: 10 of any symbol make one of the next landmark, so they are always regrouped
final_answer.spoken: no, ten of any symbol make one of the next landmark, so they are always regrouped

hold_back: No: 10 of any symbol make one of the next landmark, so they are always regrouped
maths_rules: Egyptian landmarks are 1, 10, 100, 1000, ...; each is 10 times the one before
10 x 1 = 10 and 10 x 10 = 100: ten of a landmark equal exactly one of the next
a number is written by taking as many of the biggest landmark as fit, so ten of a smaller landmark are swapped for one of the next
check: 324 = 100 + 100 + 100 + 10 + 10 + 4 has counts 3, 2 and 4, all below 10
video_script.design: One idea: ten of a symbol are always swapped for one of the next. Ten copies of a symbol slide together into one bigger symbol on the board.
